newsitem.title: UK: Indonesian rupiah remains on ropes in London trade.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah remains on ropes in London trade.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah remained on the floor in nervous London trade on Thursday after the effective float of the currency.

Foreign exchange dealers and economists said the latest casualty of Southeast Asian currency turmoil could well slide further in coming days before sound fundamentals allowed some recovery in the longer term.
By 1230 GMT the unit was trading at 2,800/2,830 against the dollar, after touching a low of 2,815, a loss of more than five percent since Wednesday.
"Now that it has gone through 2,800 it may well go to something like 2,820 in coming sessions," said Mitul Kotecha, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank.
"But further out, I don't think the fundamentals justify this and there will be some recovery -- though it may not be for a while."
One foreign exchange dealer with a European bank predicted the rupiah could pull back to 2,700 in the coming weeks.

Emerging market economists were unanimous that Bank Indonesia, the central bank, had taken the right decision in ending its system of managing the exchange rate via an intervention band in the face of speculative attacks.
"The pragmatic and sensible line is clearly to go with the market in the short-term," said Chris Portman of Australia and New Zealand Bank.
"Clearly one cannot rule out further downward pressure, but by showing it is not wedded to any specific currency target the government immediately weakens the speculative aspect of recent pressure."

Dealers said the central bank's stance would hold the key to short-term currency direction. Bank Indonesia was unlikely to engage in heavy intervention, preferring the current approach of using interest rates as the main line of defence, they said.
Indonesia, with a current account deficit of some four percent of GDP, is not seen facing the same fundamental pressures as Thailand, with a current account gap nearly twice as large.
"Indonesia is not in the same boat as Thailand," said Portman.
That should limit the downside risk for the currency and mitigate the spillover impact of this latest episode in Southeast Asian foreign exchange turmoil.
Richard Gray, analyst at Bank America in London, in any case detects a lessening knock-on effect from each successive phase of the Asian currency drama.

While the initial fall in the Thai baht caused repercussions in Eastern Europe currencies and Latin American stocks, the last week's upheaval in the Malaysian ringgit and rupiah have caused far fewer ripples.
"There seems to be a diminishing return on currency crises in Southeast Asia...we are now experiencing crisis fatigue," he said.
